label: Asbestos
summary: A mineral fibre used in buildings, heating systems and brakes, widely until the 1980s and in many countries into the 1990s or later; treat anything built before 2000 as suspect. You can't see or feel the fibres. Breathing them causes lung cancer, mesothelioma and asbestosis 10–50 years later, and every exposure adds to the risk. Intact and left alone it does little harm; broken, cut or crumbling, it releases fibres.
signs: White or grey chalky wrapping on old boiler and heating pipes
Insulation around old boilers, furnaces and water heaters
Textured 'popcorn' or swirled ceilings in older buildings
Old square vinyl floor tiles and the black glue under them
Grey corrugated or flat cement sheets on roofs, walls and sheds
Loose grey-brown or gold pebbly loft insulation (vermiculite), which may contain it
Old fire doors, heat mats, oven seals, brake pads and clutch plates
do: Assume old building materials contain asbestos unless you know otherwise
Leave damaged material alone and pick another target
If you must pass damaged material, put on a respirator, mist it with water and move through slowly
Work upwind and outdoors when you can

Mist dusty clothes with water, take them off slowly and bag them before you go back to camp; don't shake them out. Wash them on their own, wetting them first, or throw them away: whoever washes them breathes the dust too
dont: Don't break, drill, sand, saw or scrape suspect material
Don't sweep dust dry, blow it, or use a household vacuum
Don't pull pipe lagging off to get at copper
Don't carry dust into your shelter or vehicle
Don't try asbestos removal: it needs training, sealed enclosures and proper filters
ppe: A half mask with P100 (P3) filters. A disposable P100 or FFP3 only for a short, minor job; a paper dust mask is no use
Disposable coveralls (Type 5), a size too big, cuffs taped and the hood over the respirator straps

A respirator only seals on a clean-shaven face. Check it every time: on a reusable mask, cover the filters and breathe in, and it should pull in against your face; on a disposable, cup both hands over it and breathe out, and no air should escape at the edges
Never take used overalls home: bag them with the waste
firstAid: There are no symptoms at the time
Leave the area; keep your respirator on while you mist dusty clothing, take it off carefully and bag it, then wash skin and hair
Rinse dust from eyes with clean water
Tell any doctor you ever see that you were exposed; the risk adds up over a lifetime
